children.text: A property manager comparing submetering proposals can find the same promise in every brochure: digital readings, remote access, and easier billing. But a screen or wireless connection doesn't tell you whether a meter measures accurately across the flows your building uses, or whether its readings can support a bill. The useful question isn't whether a meter is digital. It's what data the meter produces, how that data is checked and handled, and whether the instrument meets the requirements for its intended use.

What Makes a Flow Meter Digital

A digital flow meter uses electronic sensing and a programmable register to turn flow into a measurement signal that can be displayed, stored, or transmitted. That's different from a purely mechanical meter, where moving parts drive dials that someone reads by sight. A digital screen can be part of the system, but the screen alone doesn't make a meter digital.

electronics

These parts don't all have to be packaged together. A meter might show a total on its register and send pulses to a data collector. Another might transmit readings digitally over a serial connection, with no large screen on the meter body. For example, an
ultrasonic flow meter
uses sound-based sensing, but whether a particular model fits your project depends on its performance and outputs, not just its sensing method.
Read the specification, not the label

When reviewing a spec sheet, look for the sensing method, register functions, output options, power requirements, and the data the meter makes available. Does it provide a cumulative total, a live flow rate, or both? Can it send readings to your building system, or does it only display them locally?
Practical rule:
Treat “digital” as a description of how the meter produces and shares information, not as proof that it's accurate, connected, or suitable for billing.
From Mechanical Dials to Electronic Registers

A mechanical meter and a digital meter can measure the same flow, but they make the result available in different ways. On a traditional meter, moving parts drive a set of dials. Someone visits the meter, reads the figures, and records them. The display itself is the main route to the measurement.

An electronic register is more like a modern car's trip computer compared with an old odometer. Both indicate distance, but the trip computer can present several readings and make information available to other systems. Similarly, electronic metering can expose a total, a flow rate, or a signal that a collector can record. The benefit depends on what the meter and the receiving system are configured to capture.

body.alt: A side-by-side comparison of an old-fashioned mechanical flow meter and a modern digital industrial flow meter.

children.text: Hybrid meters and newer sensing

Some designs combine mechanical measurement with electronic readout or a pulse output. In this arrangement, the meter can still have moving components, while electronics make its count easier to collect remotely. A pulse LED, if present, can provide a visible indication that the meter is registering flow, but it doesn't by itself confirm that data is being stored correctly or sent to the right system.

Other designs use electronic sensing methods such as ultrasonic or magnetic measurement. Depending on the meter, these technologies can support richer readings and diagnostics than a mechanical dial offers. They aren't interchangeable, though. The right choice depends on the fluid, installation conditions, operating range, maintenance expectations, and the information your building needs.

The practical distinction is simple: mechanical meters are typically read at the instrument, while electronic and hybrid meters can make measurements available as data. When comparing products, ask whether the electronic feature is only a display, a pulse output, or a communications interface. Those options solve different problems.

This can suit consumption tracking when the meter's pulse value is known and the collector is set up correctly. Ask the supplier to state what each pulse represents and how the collector handles interruptions or missing data.

Accuracy, Resolution, and Low-Flow Performance
A meter's stated accuracy doesn't necessarily describe its performance at every flow rate.
Accuracy varies across the operating range
, so a headline figure at a nominal flow may not tell you how the meter behaves when a suite is using very little water.

That matters in multi-residential buildings. A small, continuous flow from a running toilet or concealed leak may persist for long periods, while peak flow occurs when several fixtures are used together. If a meter is chosen only to handle peak demand, its behaviour at low flow may receive too little attention.

Connecting Meters to Billing and Building Systems

A meter creates a useful reading, but a building needs a path to receive and use it. That path might lead to a billing system, a building management system, or a monitoring dashboard. The output you choose affects what data is available and what equipment is needed to collect it.

water meters with remote reading
provides further context on that type of setup.

For building operations, an analogue signal such as 4–20 mA can send a flow-rate value to compatible control equipment. A facility team might use it to monitor flow in a heating or cooling circuit. With Modbus, a compatible system may retrieve more than one data point, which can support a dashboard that shows current readings alongside accumulated use.

Wireless systems offer another route. A meter can transmit to a gateway, which forwards data to software for staff or tenants. That arrangement can support remote monitoring, but it depends on the meter, communications coverage, gateway, and receiving software working together.

. The key purchasing question is still specific to your site: what value will this meter send, to which system, and who will respond when readings are missing or unexpected?
Choosing the Right Meter for Submetering

A supplier proposes a connected water meter for your suites. Before comparing screens or wireless features, define what the installation must measure and how those measurements will be used. A purchase order works like a checklist for acceptance: it should describe the measurement, the records, and the responsibilities.
Start with the medium. Water, gas, electricity, and thermal-energy measurement require equipment suited to each application. For water,
Measurement Canada's water-meter consultation report

records utility use of positive-displacement, magnetic, compound, and ultrasonic meters. These technologies have different operating characteristics; their names alone don't establish suitability for your building.

Specify performance across the expected range. Ask for low-flow performance and peak-demand limits, then document resolution, local logging intervals, and transmission intervals. Detecting a small change and retaining a usable record of it are separate requirements.
Questions to put to the supplier
What is the meter designed to measure?
Specify the medium, sensor technology, operating conditions, and approved configuration.
What data will we receive?
List the required totals, flow rates, and diagnostics, including units and recording intervals.
How are readings collected?
Assign responsibility for validation, estimation, and editing (VEE), including review of missing or unusual readings.
What compliance applies here?
Request confirmation of applicable federal, provincial, municipal, and contractual requirements, including Measurement Canada approval where applicable to the intended billing use.
Who maintains the installation?
Name who handles commissioning, ongoing checks, repair, replacement, and reverification where required.

Include shared spaces in the design when they affect consumption allocation or loss investigation. Specify how suite and common-area readings will be time-synchronized, and how records will remain traceable through meter failure or replacement.
Put those requirements in writing before ordering.
